title: Subqueries
summary: A query inside a query: as a value, as a list, and as a table.

steps.title: Pixelforge Games
body: Month three takes you to **Pixelforge**, the studio behind the space brawler *Starfall Arena*. Their producer wants answers like *"who spends more than the average player?"*, which need one answer **before** you can ask the next question.
A **subquery** is a SELECT in brackets, used inside another query. A **scalar subquery** returns one value and can go wherever a value can:
The inner query runs, returns `1050`, and the outer query becomes `WHERE gems > 1050`.

setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, handle TEXT, country TEXT, joined TEXT);
CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, player_id INTEGER REFERENCES players(id), item TEXT, gems INTEGER, day TEXT);
steps.explain: The average is 1050 gems. Only Comet Skin (1200) and the Founder Pack (4000) cost more.

steps.title: The biggest single purchase
prompt: Return the **handle**-less purchase row(s) with the **highest gems** in the table: **id**, **item**, **gems**. Use a scalar subquery with `MAX`, not `ORDER BY ... LIMIT`.
Tables: `players(id, handle, country, joined)` and `purchases(id, player_id, item, gems, day)`.
setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, handle TEXT, country TEXT, joined TEXT);
CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, player_id INTEGER REFERENCES players(id), item TEXT, gems INTEGER, day TEXT);

require.message: Uses a scalar subquery with MAX

hints: Unlike LIMIT 1, this returns every row that ties for the top.

steps.title: IN (subquery)
body: A subquery that returns **one column of many rows** can feed `IN`:
WHERE id IN (SELECT player_id FROM purchases WHERE item = 'Battle Pass');
This often reads more naturally than a join when you only need columns from the outer table, and it never duplicates rows (a player with two Battle Passes still appears once).
> **Remember the trap:** `NOT IN (subquery)` returns nothing if the subquery yields a single NULL. Prefer `NOT EXISTS` for "not in".

steps.title: Skin owners
prompt: Return the **handle** of every player who bought a **Comet Skin**. Use `IN` with a subquery.
Tables: `players(id, handle, country, joined)` and `purchases(id, player_id, item, gems, day)`.
solution: WHERE id IN (SELECT player_id FROM purchases WHERE item = 'Comet Skin');
setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, handle TEXT, country TEXT, joined TEXT);
CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, player_id INTEGER REFERENCES players(id), item TEXT, gems INTEGER, day TEXT);
hints: The subquery returns the player ids; the outer query turns them into handles.

steps.prompt: Player 3 bought three things. How many times does `lumen` appear?
code: WHERE id IN (SELECT player_id FROM purchases);
options: Once with IN, but three times with an inner JOIN to purchases
steps.explain: IN asks a yes/no question per player. A join produces one row per matching purchase.

steps.prompt: Match each subquery to the shape of result it must return.
pairs: one column, any number of rows
anything: only whether a row exists matters

steps.title: Subqueries in FROM and SELECT
body: A subquery in **FROM** is a temporary table (a *derived table*) and needs an alias:
That's an **average of totals**, two levels of aggregation, which one GROUP BY can't do.
A subquery in **SELECT** computes a value per row (here it's *correlated*: it refers to the outer row `p`, more on that next lesson):
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM purchases AS x WHERE x.player_id = p.id) AS purchases

setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, handle TEXT, country TEXT, joined TEXT);
CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, player_id INTEGER REFERENCES players(id), item TEXT, gems INTEGER, day TEXT);
steps.explain: Totals per buyer range from kestrel's 300 to oakshade's 4000. Zephyr bought nothing, so isn't in the derived table at all.

steps.title: Spending tiers
prompt: For each buyer compute their total gems spent, then count buyers per tier. Return **tier** and **buyers** where tier is `whale` (2000 or more), `regular` (1000 to 1999) or `minnow` (under 1000).
Use a derived table in FROM.
Tables: `players(id, handle, country, joined)` and `purchases(id, player_id, item, gems, day)`.
solution: FROM (SELECT player_id, SUM(gems) AS total FROM purchases GROUP BY player_id) AS t
setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, handle TEXT, country TEXT, joined TEXT);
CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, player_id INTEGER REFERENCES players(id), item TEXT, gems INTEGER, day TEXT);
hints: Inner: total per player. Outer: CASE on the total, then GROUP BY the tier.

steps.title: Above-average spenders
prompt: Return the **handle** and **total** gems of every player whose total spend is **above the average total per buyer**.
Tables: `players(id, handle, country, joined)` and `purchases(id, player_id, item, gems, day)`.
solution: JOIN (SELECT player_id, SUM(gems) AS total FROM purchases GROUP BY player_id) AS t
WHERE t.total > (SELECT AVG(total) FROM (SELECT SUM(gems) AS total FROM purchases GROUP BY player_id));
setup: CREATE TABLE players (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, handle TEXT, country TEXT, joined TEXT);
CREATE TABLE purchases (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, player_id INTEGER REFERENCES players(id), item TEXT, gems INTEGER, day TEXT);
hints: Join players to a derived table of totals.
The average per buyer is itself a subquery over that derived table: `(SELECT AVG(total) FROM (SELECT SUM(gems) AS total FROM purchases GROUP BY player_id))`.
